title: Repair: a vacuous capability refusal, a discarded protocol warning, and a drift test that can skip
description:
Three findings from the Phase 2 final review, all in the robustness work the
review otherwise called the best in the epic.

## 1. The capability half of the Start refusal is vacuous

`RequireCapability` has ZERO callers outside the client package, and
`TestTheExecutorDemandsNoCapability` (internal/exec/herdr/operational_test.go:287)
PINS that the refusal cannot arise — it asserts a herdr advertising nothing at
all runs a whole attempt.

That test is honest about today: the five operations genuinely place no
capability demand on the server. But tick jv7's acceptance asked for a
capability the server does not advertise to be "refused BY NAME at the point of
use", and an inverted test proving the refusal can never occur is not that.

Decide and log which is true, then make the code and the test agree:
- either the executor really needs no capability, and jv7's clause is amended
  with that reasoning (the AC5 precedent from Phase 1), or
- some operation does depend on one — live handoff, the detached daemon — and
  it demands it by name at the point of use.

Do not leave a passing test that proves a required behaviour is unreachable.

## 2. The above-warn protocol warning is discarded in production

client.New only emits the "newer than the protocol this client was verified
against" warning through Options.ProtocolWarning, and the executor's only
constructor (internal/exec/herdr/executor.go:161) omits the writer. So the
warning goes nowhere.

This matters NOW: the local herdr is 0.9.0 on protocol 22 against a client
verified at 20. The one signal that says so is silently dropped.

## 3. The live drift test skips when herdr is absent from PATH

yod's vocabulary contract is diffed against the live `herdr api schema --json`,
which is the right design — but a skip on an absent binary means CI proves
nothing about drift. Decide whether the epic gate requires a live herdr, and if
not, say plainly in the doc what the offline run does and does not prove.

acceptance_criteria: The capability clause is either implemented (some operation demands a capability by name at the point of use) or amended by a logged decision, and no test remains that proves a required refusal is unreachable; the above-warn protocol warning reaches an operator in production rather than being dropped by a constructor that omits the writer, shown against the local herdr 0.9.0 on protocol 22; what the drift test proves when herdr is absent is stated in the doc, and whether the epic gate requires a live herdr is a logged decision; make test-short green.
